definition: Nuclear power plants generate electricity the same basic way as coal plants — producing superheated steam to drive turbines — and, like coal plants, become more efficient at converting heat to electricity the higher their operating temperature.
core_idea: Operating temperature is a key efficiency driver for both nuclear and coal steam-turbine plants: lower-temperature plants convert roughly 25% of heat energy to electricity, while larger, hotter plants can convert 50-60%.
key_points: Nuclear power is not renewable but is presented as an alternative to fossil-fuel-based electricity generation.
Both coal and nuclear plants produce superheated steam to drive electrical turbines.
Higher operating temperature increases thermal-to-electrical conversion efficiency.
A low-temperature plant might convert about 25% of heat energy to electricity; a larger, hotter plant might convert 50-60%.
caveats: Nuclear plants are sometimes assumed to be a totally different generation technology from coal, but the source frames them as sharing the same steam-turbine efficiency dynamics.
